ctx-word.prompt: A friend says, “The word propaganda has meant lies and manipulation from day one.” According to the documents in this card, what is the best reply?
options: You are right; if the word was the name of a church body, it already meant deceit.
Wrong; in 1622 the word was the name of a church body charged with spreading the faith, and the negative charge was added later, especially around the First World War.
Wrong; the word was first coined in the twentieth century, during the First World War.
You are right; but only in German, in other languages it was neutral.
ctx-word.explain: The documents show that the congregation was founded in 1622, that the word comes from a verb meaning “to spread”, and that its political sense settled during the First World War and was at first not judgemental. The first option is tempting because it carries today’s association back into the past; but the charge of a word changes with the period. The third option shortens the word’s history wrongly: the 1622 record is there. The fourth option invents a language distinction that no document supports.

ctx-before.prompt: A student says, “There was no propaganda in 1782, because the word was not yet used in that sense.” What do you say, looking at the Franklin case?
options: Correct; a thing can only exist if it has a name.
Correct; because there was no printing press at that time.
Wrong; there was no name, but the same tricks (a false source, an invented witness, targeting a foreign public) are documented. To understand a phenomenon you look at its function, not at its name.
Wrong; because Franklin had a propaganda ministry.
ctx-before.explain: The documents show a counterfeit newspaper supplement, an invented letter and a distribution aimed at readers abroad; the naming comes later. The first option confuses the name with the thing. The second option rests on a false fact: it was precisely a printing press that produced Franklin’s supplement. The ministry in the fourth option does not exist; ministry-style organisation is the next subject of this lesson.

people-cast.prompt: Match each event or work with its year.
pairs: The founding of the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide
The Committee on Public Information in the United States
The Reich propaganda ministry in Germany
people-cast.explain: The order is 1622, 1917, 1928, 1933, 1962. The pair most often mixed up is Lasswell (1927) and Bernays (1928): one studies war propaganda, the other defends the profession, and they appear a year apart. 1622 and 1627 (the congregation and the college) also get confused, as do Creel’s 1917 committee and Bryce’s 1915 report; keep the committee as the United States’ work and the report as Britain’s.

claim-core.prompt: According to this lesson, which of the following orders is closest to the actual course of events?
options: A theory is written, states apply the theory, the word turns negative.
Scholars study propaganda, then states set up propaganda organisations.
The word turns negative, the Nazi regime uses it, then the First World War breaks out.
State propaganda organisations are set up, invented stories are exposed and the word turns negative, then the word is hidden or studied.
claim-core.explain: The documents show that the organisations (1914, 1917) came before the theoretical analyses (Lasswell 1927, Ellul 1962) and that the negative charge settled after the war. The first option reverses the order and the third one breaks the dates: the Nazi ministry is from 1933, while the war began in 1914. The “study first” order of the second option does not fit the history of Lasswell and the Institute for Propaganda Analysis: they wrote after the organisations.

concepts-terms.prompt: A radio station presents itself as the “secret” station of the other side but is in fact run by the opposing belligerent. What is it, in this lesson’s classification?
options: White propaganda; because the operator is in fact known.
Grey propaganda; because no source is stated at all.
Black propaganda; because the message is shown as coming from someone else.
Public relations; because an organisation is managing its relations with the public.
concepts-terms.explain: In black propaganda the message is shown as coming from someone else, often from a source that looks hostile. In grey propaganda the source is merely not stated or is hidden; here there is a false source identity. The white option confuses this with the real operator being known: what matters is the source shown in the message. Public relations is the name of a profession, not a colour class.

assump-myth.prompt: True or false: If a news item is entirely true, then according to this lesson it cannot count as propaganda.
assump-myth.explain: False. According to the introduction to Ellul’s translation, modern propaganda also works with half, limited or out-of-context truths; white propaganda is information whose source is shown openly, and it can be true. “Propaganda = lie” is tempting because the bad examples stick in memory; but the criterion is not truthfulness but the organised, targeted nature of the effort. On the other hand, this does not mean every true news item is propaganda: what matters is who presents it, for what purpose, and with what source.

how-wellington.prompt: A government, instead of publishing atrocity allegations in its own name, has them collected by a commission of world-renowned figures. According to the Wellington House example, what does this move aim at?
options: Making the message look neutral and respected, and so raising its credibility.
Producing the allegations more cheaply.
Skipping opinion abroad and speaking only to its own people.
Shifting responsibility after the war onto the German government.
how-wellington.explain: Lasswell treats setting up a commission as a device for delivering findings in the voice of people with international standing and a reputation for truthfulness; the aim is credibility. The second option brings in cost and the fourth the post-war period; neither is in the document. The third option is the reverse: the target was precisely opinion abroad. One more caution: Wellington House started the commission; looking independent does not mean being independent.

how-creel.prompt: Which of the following is not something confirmed by an independent source, but rests on Creel’s own account?
options: The committee’s creation by an executive order on 13 April 1917.
The appointment of the journalist George Creel as chairman.
The closing of the committee in 1919.
The volunteer speakers having given more than seven and a half million speeches.
how-creel.explain: The first three facts are in official records (the executive order, the National Archives guide). The number of speeches is Creel’s own tally in his own book and was not confirmed separately. The tempting wrong option is to assume that a figure that looks as solid as the dates is equally reliable; but a number being a number does not show that its source is independent.

how-colours.prompt: A government, without showing its own name, spreads a view through a news site that looks independent; the site does not present itself as an institution of another country. According to the three questions, what is this?
options: White; because the content may be true.
Black; because the real source is hidden.
Grey; because the real source is hidden but is not shown as someone else.
None of them; because a news site is a media outlet.
how-colours.explain: According to the second question, if the real source is hidden it is grey, and if a false other source is shown it is black; here there is no false identity, only concealment. The white option makes truthfulness the criterion, whereas the colour depends on how the source is shown. The black option confuses concealment with showing a false source. The last option forgets that the classification asks a question about the source, not about the medium. (Dictionaries may define the colours by different criteria; this lesson uses the criterion reported by Osgood.)

ev-belgium.prompt: A historian says, “The Bryce Report was an entirely invented propaganda product.” According to the documents in this card, what do you say about that sentence?
options: True; because the report came out of a propaganda organisation’s initiative.
False; because the report is the result of a flawless judicial process.
True; because none of the claims was ever confirmed.

An overgeneralisation; Horne and Kramer document some 6,500 civilian deaths and some historians judge the report largely accurate, but it rested on unsworn, anonymous depositions and some stories could not be proved.
ev-belgium.explain: Horne and Kramer document some 6,500 civilian deaths; some historians judge the report largely accurate. Even so, the report rested on unsworn, anonymous depositions and some stories could not be established. The first option equates the source being propaganda with the content being invented. The last option goes to the opposite extreme: the method was not flawless. The right way is to ask about each claim separately.

ev-corpse.prompt: In 1917, which publishing device made the newspapers’ “corpse factory” story look believable?
options: Setting two texts from two countries side by side so that they seemed to confirm one another.
Giving the story from a single source, in a single text.
Publishing the story only after the war.
An official confirmation of the story by the German government.
ev-corpse.explain: Neander and Marlin treat the printing, on the same day and side by side, of the account translated from a Belgian newspaper and the text translated from the Berlin paper as the story’s main anchor; being side by side gave an apparently independent confirmation. The second option is the reverse: the device’s power was that it did not look like a single source. The third option gets the date wrong: the story appeared in 1917. The last is wrong too: in 1925 the German government said there was no foundation.

ev-creel-word.prompt: What do the attitudes of Creel (1920) and Goebbels (1933–34) towards the word “propaganda” show in this card?
options: That both wanted to ban the word by law.
That after the war the word carried an association with deceit, and that this was noticed in two different political orders.
That the word carried a bad association only in Germany.
That propaganda was entirely given up in those years.
ev-creel-word.explain: Creel writes that the word had come to be associated with deceit in German hands; Goebbels notices that it is associated with lies in Germany and abroad. Both sensed the word’s burden. The first option invents a ban that is not there. The third option forgets that Creel was writing from the United States. The fourth option is the most dangerous: shying away from the word did not mean giving up the work; the committee and the ministry went on.

ev-bernays.prompt: Which of the following is most faithful to the text of Bernays’s 1928 book?
options: The book defends the word propaganda and at the same time introduces the profession of “public relations counsel”.
The word propaganda does not appear in the book at all; only “public relations” is used.
The book was written to defend the founding of the Nazi ministry.
The book explains that the word propaganda was negative before the First World War.
ev-bernays.explain: The book’s title is Propaganda; inside it a quotation defending the word and the professional name “public relations counsel” stand side by side. The second option falls apart at the title alone. The third option is historically impossible: the ministry was founded in 1933, the book came out in 1928. The fourth option is the opposite of what the quotation says: the quotation says the meaning turned sinister during the war.

ev-agitprop.prompt: A speaker presents to a crowd only a single idea, through a glaring event everyone knows (for example a factory accident). According to the distinction Lenin reports, what is this person?
options: A propagandist; because he is telling about an event.
A grey propagandist; because his name is not stated.
A public relations counsel; because he is defending an organisation.
An agitator; because he presents a single idea to the crowd through an event everyone knows.
ev-agitprop.explain: In Lenin’s description the agitator presents one or a few ideas to the masses through an event everyone knows, while the propagandist explains many ideas in full to a few. The first option gives event-telling to the propagandist; but the criterion is the number of ideas and the size of the audience. The second and third options mix in other classifications (profession, colour of source); the question gives no information about a source or an organisation.

ev-nazi.prompt: According to the Holocaust Encyclopedia, what set the propaganda ministry created in 1933 apart from earlier state propaganda bodies?
options: That it worked only in wartime.
That it was a novel idea for peacetime: earlier bodies had been temporary war committees or information ministries in disguise.
That it worked only towards foreign countries.
That it left the newspapers entirely independent.
ev-nazi.explain: The encyclopedia calls the ministry a novel idea for peacetime; earlier bodies were temporary war committees or disguised information ministries. The first option says the opposite. The third option is wrong: the ministry’s target was society inside Germany as well. The fourth option is untrue: the ministry controlled the press, and the Editors Law of 1933 regulated entry into the profession.

crit-ellul.prompt: According to Ellul, to which kind of propaganda is a highly educated and informed readership more vulnerable?
options: Agitation propaganda; because it is emotional.
To none; because education is a sure protection against propaganda.
Integration propaganda; because they share society’s stereotypes and myths.
Only to black propaganda.
crit-ellul.explain: Ellul writes that integration propaganda works better in comfortable and informed milieus and that intellectuals are more sensitive to it because they share a society’s stereotypes. The first option is tempting because agitation looks emotional; but Ellul finds agitation easier with the less educated. The second option is exactly the “education protects” belief that Ellul opposes. The last option confuses the colour classification with Ellul’s distinction.

crit-whose.prompt: True or false: According to Osgood, the negative charge of the word “propaganda” arose mainly from the propaganda of the dictatorships of the 1930s.
crit-whose.explain: False. Osgood argues that the negative charge arose after the First World War, from the exposure of the invented atrocity stories of a democracy (Britain); Creel’s hesitation in 1920 and the quotation Bernays reports in 1928 fit that order. The statement is tempting because we associate the word most with Nazi propaganda; but that reverses the order of events: when the Nazi ministry was founded in 1933, the word’s bad name was already established (Goebbels’s hesitation is a sign of it).

today-computational.prompt: A news site shares an “eyewitness” story circulating from an account you have never heard of. From this lesson’s corpse-factory case, what should be your first check?
options: How emotional is the story, and how widely has it been shared?
Does the person telling it present himself as trustworthy enough?
How many people follow the site sharing it?
Where did the story first appear, and is there an independent second source?
today-computational.explain: In the corpse case the story gained the look of independent sourcing through two texts set side by side; the question to ask was the first place of appearance and a truly independent second source. The first option measures emotional force and circulation, but convincing stories by nature have both. The second and third options measure how the source looks, not whether it is right.

today-lab.prompt: The words “Kultur” on the club and “militarism” on the helmet in Poster 1 fit which of the seven devices best?
options: Testimonial; because a respected person gives approval.
Plain Folks; because the speaker talks like an ordinary person.
Name Calling; because a bad label is attached to the enemy.
Card Stacking; because only one side of the information is given.
today-lab.explain: Name Calling is attaching a bad label to an idea or object so that it is rejected without examining the evidence; the “brute” image and the labelled club and helmet fit that. Testimonial and Plain Folks leave no trace in the poster: no endorser and no ordinary person speaks. Card Stacking is the selection of information; the poster gives an image, not information, so the nearest option is Name Calling. (Fear is an extra element that has no name in the list.)

today-lab2.prompt: In Example C (ministry volunteers who do not put their identity forward), which of the five questions decides the case most?
options: Whether the source is visible (question 1).
How many words the text has.
Whether the text is emotional (question 5) on its own.
The number of recipients.
today-lab2.explain: What separates C from B is that the volunteers’ identity is not fully shown: this makes the source question decisive and slides the example towards grey. Length and the number of recipients are irrelevant to this classification. Emotionality cannot decide alone, because an honest campaign like A can also be emotional; the criterion is a set of criteria, not the answer to a single question.

turkey-ancyra.prompt: Which of the following is a documented detail supporting a reading of the Res Gestae as state communication?
options: That the same text was copied on the walls of many temples across the empire.
That Turkish houses were built against the temple in Ankara.
That the first to announce the inscription to the West was an ambassador.
That the temple still stands today.
turkey-ancyra.explain: The copying of the text on many temples suggests a centrally planned effort at spreading it, and this is a documented detail. The Turkish houses, the ambassador’s identity and the temple’s present state tell the text’s later life, not the inscription’s original purpose. That is why these options are tempting (they are all interesting details) but they do not answer the question, which is about how the inscription was used.

exam-patterns.prompt: A multiple-choice question: “How did the corpse-factory story end in 1925?” Which is the right option?
options: The British government officially confirmed the story.
The story was tried in a court in Germany.
The British government accepted, in the House of Commons, the German government’s denial that there was ever any foundation for the story.
The story was published for the first time in 1925.
exam-patterns.explain: On 2 December 1925 Foreign Secretary Chamberlain reported that the German Chancellor had authorised him to say, on the authority of the German Government, that there was never any foundation for the story, and he accepted the denial on behalf of the British Government. The first option says the opposite. The second option is invented. The fourth option shifts the date: the story was published in 1917. In an exam watch for the year slip: 1917 (publication), 1925 (withdrawal).

exam-answer.prompt: A student begins an answer with “Propaganda is a technique of lying used by the Nazis.” Which correction should they add first?
options: Goebbels’s year of birth.
The population of Berlin.
How many books Bernays wrote.
That the word was the name of a church body in 1622, that its political sense settled in the First World War, and that its negative charge was acquired after the war.
exam-answer.explain: The sentence has two basic errors: it confines the word to a Nazi-and-later history, and it equates it with lying. The fourth option corrects both. The other options are details unrelated to the subject. When you improve an answer, correct the claim itself first and the decorative information after.

summary.prompt: True or false: According to this lesson, the Creel Committee openly called its work “propaganda”.
summary.explain: False. In 1920 Creel writes that they did not call the committee’s work propaganda, because in German hands the word had come to be associated with deceit and corruption. The trap: what the committee did is studied today under the heading of propaganda; but its own naming was different.

quiz.prompt: A textbook says, “The word propaganda comes from a body of cardinals founded in Rome in 1627.” What is the best way to check this date?
options: If it is written in the book, that is enough.
Knowing that the word is Latin is enough.
Look at the institution’s own page and at an independent encyclopedia: the congregation was founded in 1622, and 1627 is the date of the college attached to it.
The date does not matter.
quiz.explain: The Vatican page says the congregation was founded in 1622 by a bull of 22 June; 1627 is the date when Pope Urban VIII founded the school attached to the congregation (the Collegium Urbanum). The first option means trusting a single source; even a 1928 book can carry this mistake through quotation. The fourth option ignores what a date is for in this lesson.

quiz.prompt: True or false: In his book Creel openly called the work of the Committee on Public Information “propaganda”.
quiz.explain: False. In 1920 Creel writes that they did not call it propaganda, because in German hands the word had come to be associated with deceit and corruption. The tempting thought is to carry over to the committee’s own naming the fact that its work is called propaganda today.

quiz.prompt: Match each concept with its definition.
pairs: The source is not stated or is hidden
The message is shown as coming from someone else
Short-lived and explosive; sets energy in motion
Slow; a deep shaping that fits a person to society’s patterns
quiz.explain: The colours measure how the source is shown; Ellul’s pair measures the duration and depth of the effect. The pair most often confused is grey and black: grey hides, black shows a false source. The second common confusion is between Ellul’s and Lenin’s use of “agitation”: in Lenin the criterion is the number of ideas and the size of the audience.

quiz.prompt: Put these events in order from earliest to latest.
items: The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide is founded (1622)
The British cabinet approves an organisation for propaganda abroad (5 September 1914)
The Committee on Public Information is created in the United States (13 April 1917)
The House of Commons accepts the denial of the corpse story (2 December 1925)
The Reich propaganda ministry is created in Germany (13 March 1933)
quiz.explain: The order is 1622, 1914, 1917, 1925, 1928, 1933, 1962. The commonest mistake is to confuse the withdrawal of the corpse story (1925) with its publication (1917). The logic: the word first, war organisations next, withdrawal and defence in the 1920s, the regime ministry in 1933, the sociological analysis last.

quiz.text: The lawyers who took down the {{1}} depositions submitted to the Bryce Committee had {{2}} authority to administer an oath; Horne and Kramer documented that about {{3}} Belgian and French civilians were killed in the 1914 invasion.

options: about 120
more than 1,200
more than 12,000
no
the
disputed

quiz.explain: The Bryce Report has more than 1,200 depositions; the lawyers had no authority to administer an oath, and witnesses’ names were left out. Horne and Kramer document some 6,500 Belgian and French civilian deaths; the options 650 and 65,000 get the order of magnitude wrong. The figure also shows that the picture was mixed: real violence occurred, but unverifiable stories circulated too.

quiz.scenario: In one country there is a site called “Citizen News” that gives the impression of being run by independent volunteers. It later becomes clear that the site is funded by a ministry and that its editors are ministry employees. The site has published a story, resting on a single eyewitness, that a neighbouring country “threatens babies”; the story appears in no other source. (Hypothetical scenario.)

parts.prompt: By this lesson’s criterion (as reported by Osgood), what colour is the site?
options: White
Grey
Black
parts.explain: The real source (the ministry) is hidden, but the site is not presented as belonging to someone else, for example the enemy: that is grey. For white the source would have to be shown correctly. Black requires the message to be presented as coming from someone else; it would be black if the site behaved like an institution of the neighbouring country.

parts.prompt: From the corpse-factory case, what should the first check be?
options: How emotional is the story?
How widely is the site shared?
Where did the story first appear, and is there an independent second source?
parts.explain: The corpse story gained the look of independent confirmation through two texts set side by side; here the story already rests on a single eyewitness. Emotionality and share counts are already high in convincing stories; what tells them apart is the structure of the sources.

parts.prompt: If the story turned out to be invented, what could be said about other reports on the same site?
options: Nothing can be said; each claim has to be tested separately.
All of them are invented too.
All of them are true, because a single mistake does not affect the whole.
parts.explain: In Belgium there were both real massacres and unverifiable stories; after the war, the ones found to be invented discredited the whole account. This shows that both shortcuts, “all lies” and “all true”, are wrong.

quiz.takeaway: Ask separately about the source’s colour (who, and whether the one shown is real) and about the claim’s chain of appearance (first place, independent second source); then test every claim one by one.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is most accurate about Bernays’s 1928 book?
options: The book defends the word propaganda and at the same time introduces the profession of “public relations counsel”.
The book uses only the phrase “public relations” instead of propaganda.
The book was written to defend the founding of the Nazi ministry.
The book examines the Bryce Report.
quiz.explain: The book is titled Propaganda; inside it a quotation defending the word and the professional name “public relations counsel” stand side by side. The third option is historically impossible: the ministry was founded in 1933. The fourth option has nothing to do with the book’s subject.

quiz.prompt: According to Ellul, in which milieu does integration propaganda work better?
options: Among those with little education and information, because they are easily fooled.
Only on the radio.
Only in wartime.
In comfortable, cultivated and informed milieus, because they share society’s stereotypes.
quiz.explain: Ellul writes that integration propaganda works better in cultivated and informed milieus and that intellectuals are more sensitive to it than peasants; the less educated are more open to agitation. The first option mixes the two up. The second and third options are limits that are not Ellul’s criterion.

quiz.prompt: What happened in the House of Commons in 1925 about the “corpse factory” story?
options: The story was officially confirmed.
Foreign Secretary Chamberlain accepted on behalf of the British Government the German Government’s denial that there was ever any foundation for the story.
The story was taken to court in Germany.
The story was published for the first time that day.
quiz.explain: On 2 December 1925 Chamberlain reported that the German Chancellor had authorised him to say, on the authority of the German Government, that there was never any foundation for the story, and he accepted the denial on behalf of the British Government. The first and fourth options are wrong in date and content; the story had been published in 1917.

quiz.prompt: Who was the priority audience of the bureau for propaganda abroad that Britain set up in 1914 (Wellington House)?
options: The German people.
The British people.
Opinion abroad, above all American opinion.
The people of the Ottoman State.
quiz.explain: Sources say Wellington House gave priority to American opinion; the cabinet decision, too, concerned informing and influencing opinion abroad. The first option names the enemy’s people; but the bureau’s documented focus was opinion abroad. The second option confuses it with the home front; the bureau faced outward. The fourth option is supported by no document.
